## Today’s goals

By the end of this session, you should be able to:

- Build a small, trustworthy practical-AI learning network.
- Match instructors and sources to different learning goals.
- Evaluate tutorials for evidence, currency, incentives, and safety.
- Use YouTube and Facebook without confusing popularity with authority.
- Turn passive viewing into a reproducible practice routine.

## Practical AI is several subjects

| Goal | What to learn |
|---|---|
| Use AI well | Prompting, context, verification, privacy |
| Build with models | APIs, structured output, tool use, evaluation |
| Work with data | Statistics, R/Python, visualization, reproducibility |
| Use coding agents | Git, tests, permissions, sandboxes, review |
| Understand models | Neural networks, training, inference, limitations |
| Teach responsibly | Learning design, accessibility, policy, assessment |

No single creator is best for every layer.

## Use a source ladder

Prefer evidence in this order when checking a factual claim:

1. Official documentation and release notes
2. Original research or technical report
3. Maintainer explanation or reproducible example
4. Independent expert analysis
5. Tutorial or course
6. Social-media summary
7. Unsourced screenshot or viral claim

A useful teacher can simplify a topic. The original source still decides product syntax and current policy.

## Andrew Ng and DeepLearning.AI

[DeepLearning.AI](https://www.deeplearning.ai/) is a strong starting point for structured introductions to machine learning, generative AI, and practical model use.

Why follow:

- Short courses and longer learning sequences
- Clear conceptual framing
- Material from Andrew Ng and invited practitioners
- Coverage from foundations to current tools

Use the courses to establish vocabulary, then reproduce examples outside the course environment.

## Jeremy Howard and fast.ai

[fast.ai](https://www.fast.ai/) emphasizes learning by building useful models early and studying theory alongside practice.

Why follow:

- Free course materials
- Notebook-based experimentation
- Strong attention to practical model training
- Open-source library and community

Best fit: learners ready to write Python and inspect working code rather than only watch demonstrations.

## Ethan Mollick

Ethan Mollick’s [One Useful Thing](https://www.oneusefulthing.org/) examines how generative AI changes work, teaching, and organizations.

Why follow:

- Frequent hands-on experiments
- Attention to education and workplace implications
- Clear separation between observed behavior and broader interpretation
- Practical prompts and workflow ideas

Treat any rapidly changing product observation as time-stamped evidence, not a permanent capability statement.

## Simon Willison

[Simon Willison](https://simonwillison.net/) documents language models, tools, security issues, and experiments in unusually reproducible detail.

Why follow:

- Links to primary sources
- Small executable examples
- Careful attention to prompt injection and data boundaries
- Ongoing notes about model and tool releases

Best fit: technically curious readers who want to understand how claims were tested.

## Josh Starmer and StatQuest

[StatQuest](https://statquest.org/) by Josh Starmer provides approachable explanations of statistics and machine-learning concepts.

Why follow:

- Visual, step-by-step explanations
- Strong coverage of statistical foundations
- Clear distinctions among related methods
- Useful preparation before implementing an algorithm

Use conceptual videos together with an R or Python example and an interpretation exercise.

## Grant Sanderson and 3Blue1Brown

[3Blue1Brown](https://www.3blue1brown.com/) uses mathematical visualization to build intuition for topics such as linear algebra, calculus, probability, and neural networks.

Why follow:

- Excellent geometric intuition
- Carefully designed visual explanations
- Useful foundation for understanding model mechanics

Visual intuition should complement—not replace—definitions, calculations, and empirical checks.

## Posit and the R community

For AI work involving R and reproducible data science, use:

- [Posit videos](https://posit.co/resources/videos/) and official product documentation
- [R for Data Science](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/)
- [tidymodels](https://www.tidymodels.org/) documentation
- Package websites and release notes
- Conference talks whose code and data are available

This keeps model use connected to data quality, statistical reasoning, and reproducible reporting.

## Official channels still matter

Follow the documentation and release channels for tools you actually use:

- OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Microsoft, Meta, and model providers
- Quarto, R, Python, Jupyter, and Posit
- Coding-agent and harness repositories
- University IT and privacy guidance

Official sources may be promotional, but they remain authoritative for supported syntax, pricing, limits, and policy.

## How to evaluate a YouTube tutorial

Before following it, check:

- Publication date and software version
- Links to code, data, and primary documentation
- Whether installation commands are explained
- Whether the presenter shows failures and verification
- Whether costs, affiliate links, or sponsorships are disclosed
- Whether private information appears on screen
- Whether the final artifact can be reproduced

A polished demo can hide setup, retries, editing, or paid access.

## How to use Facebook communities

Facebook groups can help with discovery, peer support, and local teaching ideas.

Use them carefully:

- Prefer moderated groups with clear rules and searchable archives.
- Check the author’s identity and original source.
- Do not download unknown executables or browser extensions.
- Never paste API keys, student data, or unpublished research.
- Be skeptical of urgent offers, guaranteed income, and secret prompts.
- Move technical claims to official documentation before acting.

Facebook is a conversation layer—not the final source of truth.

## Red flags in AI-learning content {.compact}

- “This tool is completely private” without a data-flow explanation
- “Free forever” without limits or a business model
- “One prompt replaces expertise”
- Benchmark claims without data, settings, or baselines
- Installation commands piped directly into a shell without inspection
- Advice to disable all permissions or antivirus protections
- Screenshots presented without links or dates
- Confident claims that prediction proves causation
- A course built mostly around referral links

## Build a balanced learning network

Choose a small portfolio:

| Role | Example source type |
|---|---|
| Foundations | StatQuest, 3Blue1Brown, a textbook |
| Structured course | DeepLearning.AI or fast.ai |
| Current analysis | One Useful Thing or Simon Willison |
| Software truth | Official documentation and release notes |
| Data workflow | Posit, R4DS, tidymodels, Quarto |
| Peer community | A well-moderated local or online group |

Following fewer sources deeply is often better than following dozens passively.

## Turn a video into practice

For each useful tutorial:

1. Write the learning claim in one sentence.
2. Locate the primary documentation.
3. Reproduce the smallest example.
4. Change one input or assumption.
5. Record what failed and why.
6. Explain the result in your own words.
7. Save code, versions, and links.
8. Create one question for another learner.

Watching feels fluent; reproduction reveals understanding.

## A weekly learning routine

### 30 minutes: foundations

Study one statistical, mathematical, or programming concept.

### 30 minutes: current tool

Read official documentation and test one feature.

### 30 minutes: build

Create a tiny artifact using public or synthetic data.

### 15 minutes: verify and reflect

Check claims, document versions, and note what remains uncertain.

## Mini-activity: audit a tutorial

Select one AI tutorial or social-media post and score it from 0–2 on:

1. Currency
2. Primary-source links
3. Reproducibility
4. Cost disclosure
5. Privacy and security guidance
6. Evidence for claims
7. Clear audience and prerequisites

**Decision:** follow, adapt cautiously, or skip?

## Key takeaways {.compact}

- Build a learning network with foundations, practical instruction, current analysis, official documentation, and peer support.
- Andrew Ng, Jeremy Howard, Ethan Mollick, Simon Willison, Josh Starmer, and Grant Sanderson serve different learning needs.
- YouTube is excellent for explanation; Facebook is useful for community; neither replaces primary sources.
- Reproduce examples, change assumptions, and preserve evidence instead of collecting tips passively.
